s: Helen is accused of Helen's guilt and innocence (Menelaus and Hecuba judge her guilty, while she pleads innocence)
q: And is it granted that I speak, or no, In answer to them ere I die, to show I die most wronged and innocent?

s: Helen attributes her abduction to Aphrodite (in her defense before Menelaus)
q: my love Hath holpen Hellas. No fierce Eastern crown Is o'er your lands, no spear hath cast them down. O, it was well for Hellas! But for me Most ill; caught up and sold across the sea For this my beauty

s: Helen is accused of causing the Trojan War (through her departure with Paris)
q: And after, when Thou camest here to Troy, and in thy track Argos and all its anguish and the rack Of war

s: Hecuba is a queen (queen of Troy and mother of Paris)
q: O Queen, think of thy children and thy land, And break her spell!

s: Hecuba is mother of Paris (his mother by birth)
q: cometh first, who bare the seed and well Of springing sorrow, when to life she brought Paris

s: Hecuba opposes Helen (as Helen's accuser and enemy)
q: Slay this woman, and upraise The law for evermore: she that betrays Her husband's bed, let her be judged and die.

s: Hecuba advocates Helen's execution (to uphold justice and punish betrayal)
q: Be true, O King; let Hellas bear her crown Of Justice. Slay this woman

s: Paris is a son of Hecuba (born to the Trojan royal house)
q: cometh first, who bare the seed and well Of springing sorrow, when to life she brought Paris

s: Paris is a beautiful man (famously attractive among his peers)
q: My son was passing beautiful, beyond His peers

s: Menelaus commands Greek army (as armed ministers)
q: Ye soldiers! Up into the chambers where She croucheth! Grip the long blood-reeking hair, And drag her to mine eyes

s: Paris is judged by the three goddesses' judgment (beneath the trees on Mount Ida)
q: this Paris judged beneath the trees Three Crowns of Life, three diverse Goddesses.

s: the three goddesses' judgment concerns Hera (Hera offers royal sovereignty)
q: Hera held a Throne-- If majesties he craved--to reign alone From Phrygia to the last realm of the West.

s: the three goddesses' judgment concerns Pallas Athena (Pallas offers military conquest)
q: The gift of Pallas was of War, to lead His East in conquering battles, and make bleed The hearths of Hellas.

s: the three goddesses' judgment concerns Aphrodite (Aphrodite offers Paris Helen's love)
q: And Cypris, if he deemed her loveliest, Beyond all heaven, made dreams about my face And for her grace gave me.

s: the Trojan War is caused by Helen (in the Greek and Trojan account)
q: And after, when Thou camest here to Troy, and in thy track Argos and all its anguish and the rack Of war

s: Troy contains the Trojan huts (where the captives are kept)
q: Here with the prisoners They keep her, in these huts, among the hordes Of numbered slaves.

s: Greeks awards Helen (to Menelaus after the Greek victory)
q: The host whose labouring swords Won her, have given her up to me

s: Women of Troy mourns the sacrifice of Troy (lamenting the loss of the city's rites and temples)
q: And hast thou turned from the Altar of frankincense, And given to the Greek thy temple of Ilion? The flame of the cakes of corn, is it gone from hence, The myrrh on the air and the wreathed towers gone?

s: Menelaus possesses Greek fleet (as their king and commander)
q: And when there come Fair breezes, my long ships shall bear her home.

s: the Trojan captives' exile carries me (over the bitter brine)
q: and me the ships Shall bear o'er the bitter brine, Storm-birds upon angry pinions

s: Helen's execution faces some pitiless doom (in Argos)
q: And when we come To Argos, then . . . O then some pitiless doom Well-earned, black as her heart!

s: marital faithfulness is violated by Helen (in Hecuba's accusation)
q: she that betrays Her husband's bed

s: the sea voyage to Greece carries me (over the bitter brine)
q: and me the ships Shall bear o'er the bitter brine

s: Helen's beauty is a birthright (regarded by Helen as both potential glory and stigma)
q: And this one birthright of my beauty, this That might have been my glory, lo, it is A stamp that God hath burned, of slavery!

s: Menelaus seeks Helen's execution (as punishment for her alleged betrayal)
q: I seek To kill thee, woman; not to hear thee speak!

s: Menelaus rejects Helen's alleged enchantment (as an explanation of her conduct)
q: And all her fair Tale of enchantment, 'tis a thing of air!

s: Menelaus enforces marital faithfulness (through Helen's punishment)
q: One that shall bind Once for all time the law on womankind Of faithfulness!

s: Helen is a captive (held among the Trojan prisoners)
q: Here with the prisoners They keep her, in these huts, among the hordes Of numbered slaves.

s: Helen is wife of Menelaus (whose wife she was and whom she still calls husband)
q: That was my wife.

s: Helen is associated with Helen's beauty (her beauty is treated as the source of her power and disgrace)
q: And this one birthright of my beauty, this That might have been my glory, lo, it is A stamp that God hath burned, of slavery!

s: Astyanax is buried in Hector's shield (as his last house)
q: Child, they have left thee beggared of all else In Hector's house; but one thing shalt thou keep, This war-shield bronzen-barred, wherein to sleep.

s: Astyanax has a grave Astyanax's grave
q: Go, women: lay our dead In his low sepulchre.

s: Astyanax's death is a Greek killing (motivated by fear)
q: 'There lieth here A babe whom the Greeks feared, and in their fear Slew him.'

s: Hecuba is the mother of Hector
q: And thou, grey Mother, Mother-Shield that bore A thousand days of glory, thy last crown Is here. . . . Dear Hector's shield!

s: Hecuba is the grandmother of Astyanax
q: At daybreak, when he crept into my bed, Called me kind names, and promised: 'Grandmother, When thou art dead, I will cut close my hair, And lead out all the captains to ride by Thy tomb.'

s: Hecuba mourns Astyanax (as his grandmother)
q: Old, homeless, childless, that for thee must shed Cold tears, so young, so miserably dead.

s: Hecuba is enslaved to Odysseus (chosen as his allotted captive)
q: Follow: Odysseus' men be here, and wait To guide thee. . . . 'Tis to him thou go'st for thrall.

s: Hecuba leaves my land
q: I go forth from my land, and all its ways Are filled with fire!

s: Andromache is the mother of Astyanax
q: 'Tis she hath charmed these tears into mine eyes, Weeping her fatherland, as o'er the wave She gazed, and speaking words to Hector's grave. Howbeit, she prayed us that due rites be done For burial of this babe, thine Hector's son

s: Andromache is captive of Pyrrhus (taken as his prize and carried to Thessaly)
q: Loath enough before Was he to linger, and now goes the more In haste, bearing Andromache, his prize.

s: Hector is the father of Astyanax
q: For burial of this babe, thine Hector's son

s: Hector possesses Hector's shield (his battle shield)
q: This war-shield bronzen-barred, wherein to sleep. Alas, thou guardian true of Hector's fair Left arm

s: Hector's shield is a war shield (bronze-fronted and battle-worn)
q: And, lo! this great bronze-fronted shield, the dread Of many a Greek, that Hector held in fray

s: Hector's shield protects Astyanax (as his burial covering)
q: Child, they have left thee beggared of all else In Hector's house; but one thing shalt thou keep, This war-shield bronzen-barred, wherein to sleep.

s: Priam lies Hecuba
q: Priam, mine own Priam, Lying so lowly

s: Odysseus owns Hecuba (as an allotted slave)
q: She was his lot Chosen from all and portioned.

s: Pyrrhus carries Andromache (as his prize to Thessaly)
q: In haste, bearing Andromache, his prize.

s: Greeks kill Astyanax (by throwing him from Ilion's tower)
q: Our prince, whom bitter Greeks this hour Have hurled to death from Ilion's tower.

s: Talthybius delivers Astyanax (dead, to Hecuba)
q: And in thine hands She bade me lay him, to be swathed in bands Of death and garments, such as rest to thee In these thy fallen fortunes

s: Trojan women goes to slavery
q: Farewell!--O spirit grey, Whatso is coming, Fail not from under me. Weak limbs, why tremble ye? Forth where the new long day Dawneth to slavery!

s: Troy is fallen land
q: For fear this babe some day might raise again His fallen land!

s: Troy is destroyed by fire (during its final destruction)
q: The land crieth for death: O stormy battlements that red fire hath riven

s: Troy is no more vanished city (after its walls collapse)
q: And the cloud is northward, southward; Troy is gone for ever!

s: Troy's walls is wounded City (with fiery hands and torches)
q: Fiery hands in the dusk, and a shock Of torches flung! What lingereth still O wounded City

s: fire destroys Troy (burning the city from its heart)
q: Up, fling the fire into her heart!

s: fall of Troy causes enslavement of the Trojan women
q: the flame Hath thee, and we, thy children, pass away To slavery

s: divine fate turns us (in His hand)
q: Had He not turned us in His hand, and thrust Our high things low and shook our hills as dust, We had not been this splendour, and our wrong An everlasting music for the song Of earth and heaven!

s: Greek trumpet signals Trojan women (their departure for the Greek ships)
q: And ye--so hath one word two faces--stand, Daughters of Troy, till on your ruined wall The echo of my master's trumpet call In signal breaks: then, forward to the sea, Where the long ships lie waiting.

s: Talthybius reports that Andromache (has been taken as Pyrrhus's prize)
q: Loath enough before Was he to linger, and now goes the more In haste, bearing Andromache, his prize.

s: Talthybius orders Greek captains (to burn Troy)
q: Ye Captains that have charge to wreck this keep Of Priam's City, let your torches sleep No more! Up, fling the fire into her heart!

s: Astyanax is a prince of Troy (Hector's son)
q: Our prince, whom bitter Greeks this hour Have hurled to death from Ilion's tower.

s: Astyanax is a dead child
q: And, lo! this great bronze-fronted shield, the dread Of many a Greek, that Hector held in fray, O never in God's name--so did she pray-- Be this borne forth to hang in Peleus' hall Or that dark bridal chamber, that the wall May hurt her eyes; but here, in Troy o'erthrown, Instead of cedar wood and vaulted stone, Be this her child's last house.

s: Astyanax is killed by Greeks (thrown to death from Ilion's tower)
q: Our prince, whom bitter Greeks this hour Have hurled to death from Ilion's tower.

s: Astyanax is fevred by Greeks (because of a possible future restoration of Troy)
q: For fear this babe some day might raise again His fallen land!

l: The Electra of Euripides, The Electra of Euripides, Introduction[1]
s: The introduction presents Euripides' Electra as a realistic, tightly constructed, intellectual, and rebellious tragedy that challenges conventional classicism. It compares Euripides' treatment of the legend of Orestes and Electra with those of Aeschylus and Sophocles, focusing on the moral horror of matricide and the role of Apollo's command. Euripides portrays Orestes and especially Electra as psychologically damaged real people rather than heroic or villainous figures. Electra is identified as the tragedy's central character: a woman consumed by grief, hatred, love, poverty, frustrated ambition, and the loss of her youth.

l: Electra of Euripides, The Electra of Euripides, Introduction[1]
s: The Electra of Euripides is described as a close-knit, powerful, well-constructed, realistic, intellectual, and rebellious tragedy. It examines the psychological and moral problems involved in Orestes and Electra's deliberate murder of their mother.

l: Euripides, The Electra of Euripides, Introduction[1]
s: Euripides is presented as carrying Aeschylus' intellectual treatment of the story a step further. He regards the mother-murder as a sin and horror that should not have been committed, and he portrays its perpetrators as psychologically damaged real people.

l: ancient tragedies, The Electra of Euripides, Introduction[1]
s: Ancient tragedies are said to have drawn on history as legend for a fifth-century Greek audience. Three extant tragedies concerning Orestes, Electra, and the murder of Clytemnestra are identified: Aeschylus' The Libation-Bearers, Euripides' Electra, and Sophocles' Electra.

l: The Libation-Bearers, The Electra of Euripides, Introduction[1]
s: The Libation-Bearers, by Aeschylus and dated to 456 B.C., is identified as one of three extant tragedies based on the legend of Orestes and Electra.

l: Sophocles' Electra, The Electra of Euripides, Introduction[1]
s: Sophocles' Electra, whose date is unknown but may make it the latest of the three related tragedies, preserves an atmosphere similar to Homer's. It presents Orestes as healthy and free from doubt or conscience, and treats the matricide in a manner praised by Schlegel as classical and austere.

l: the legend of Orestes and Electra, The Electra of Euripides, Introduction[1]
s: The legend tells how Agamemnon's son and daughter eventually killed their guilty mother and her paramour in revenge, following Apollo's express command. Homer, Aeschylus, Euripides, and Sophocles treat the story in notably different moral and psychological styles.

l: Agamemnon, The Electra of Euripides, Introduction[1]
s: Agamemnon is the murdered king whose son and daughter avenge him by killing their mother and her paramour. His death provides the central wrong around which the legend and the tragedies are organized.

l: Orestes, The Electra of Euripides, Introduction[1]
s: Orestes is Agamemnon's exiled son, bred in desperate hopes of restoration and driven by a savage doctrine of revenge confirmed by an oracle. He is very young, vulnerable to overpowering impulses and periods of brooding, and is swept away by Electra's more intense nature.

l: Electra, The Electra of Euripides, Introduction[1]
s: Electra is the central figure of Euripides' tragedy. Shattered by childhood trauma, she is haunted by hatred for her mother and stepfather and love for her dead father and exiled brother; she also resents poverty, remembers former luxury and status, and feels her youth passing.

l: Clytemnestra, The Electra of Euripides, Introduction[1]
s: Clytemnestra is the guilty mother whom Orestes and Electra kill in revenge for Agamemnon's murder. In the comparison of the tragedians, Aeschylus' Clytemnestra is mentioned as less profoundly studied than Euripides' Electra.

l: Aegisthus, The Electra of Euripides, Introduction[1]
s: Aegisthus is Agamemnon's paramour and one of the guilty figures killed by Orestes and Electra. In Sophocles' treatment, he is driven into the house to receive an especially ignominious death.
